title: Parvati's tapas
hookLine: a young ascetic visits Parvati in the forest and mocks the god she loves, and she won't stay to listen
carry: parvati won shiva by tapas, not looks
last: ONE WORD CAN CHANGE THE WORLD.

cards: A princess has left her father's palace in the Himalayas for the forest. She tried to win the great ascetic Shiva the ordinary way: beauty, flowers, the god of love himself taking aim at Shiva. It went badly.
Shiva opened his third eye, burned the god of love to ash, and walked away. So the princess changes her plan. If Shiva lives by austerity, she will out-austere him.
In Kalidasa's poem, The Birth of Kumara, that's where we find her: alone in the forest, taking up the life of an ascetic. Today, Parvati.

teach.b: Kalidasa describes her austerity season by season: standing among fires in the summer heat, in cold water through winter nights, living on less and less, until she gives up eating even fallen leaves.
That, the poem says, is why those who know the old stories call her Aparna, the one without even a leaf.
One day a visitor comes: a young ascetic with matted hair. He asks why someone so lovely is doing all this. When he learns it's for Shiva, he starts, very gently, to make fun of her choice.
Shiva? Who wears snakes and ash, rides an old bull, haunts cremation grounds? Nobody even knows his family.
A princess like you, with him? Parvati doesn't laugh along, and she doesn't crumble. She defends Shiva point by point, then does something sharper.

She tells her companion to stop him, because whoever speaks badly of a great soul does wrong, and so does whoever stays and listens. And she turns to walk away. Then the young ascetic drops the disguise.

He was Shiva all along, testing her. In the poem he says that from now on he's hers, won by her austerity. This is tapas, one of Hinduism's big words: heat, the fire of discipline, austerity offered up.
Parvati's tapas isn't punishment; it's devotion that won't quit. Beauty failed. Steady devotion won the lord of yogis.
And it's why, in parts of India, women keep the Hartalika Teej fast in her name, many going without food and even water for the day, praying as she did.

how: Parvati's austerity to win Shiva is remembered in festivals such as Hartalika Teej, when some Hindu women fast and pray in her honor, and her story is told in the Puranas and in Kalidasa's poem.

s: Parvati wins Shiva because the god of love's arrow works
Shiva burns the god of love to ash; she wins him through her own austerity.
Parvati walks away rather than keep listening to Shiva being mocked
she says the listener does wrong too, and turns to leave.
Parvati's tapas is a punishment she gives herself
it's devotion offered up: discipline kept for the one she loves, until Shiva himself comes.

games.q: you're Parvati, deep in your austerity. a polite young ascetic tells you Shiva is ash-covered, snake-wearing and of no known family. what do you do?
o: agree, and go home to the palace
defend Shiva, then turn to walk away
games.why: she defends him and says the listener does wrong too, and turns to go. then the ascetic drops the disguise: it was Shiva, testing her.

practice: Hindus keep tapas in small, everyday forms: a vrat, a vow, like a fast on a set day of the week, or a mantra said every morning no matter what. Choose one small vow for this week.
If you pray, offer it to Parvati or God; if you don't, keep it steady anyway, as Parvati did.

wordCard.voice: Durga. The name over these five; and some Hindus hear Parvati and Durga as one Goddess in two moods: the patient one in the forest, the warrior on the lion. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Aparna. Kalidasa says those who know the old stories call Parvati this because she gave up even fallen leaves.
